kf1.tip: Link cells → tissues → organs → organ systems → organism to Cell Structure and Microscopy. Say which level that lesson studied and how it builds the next level.
kf1.note: Cell Structure and Microscopy studied the first level, the cell. Cells are the building blocks of everything above them. Cells with a similar structure and function group together to form a tissue. Different tissues then combine to form an organ, such as the stomach. If you started at tissues or organs, you missed that the cell is the base level that the whole hierarchy builds on.

kf2.tip: Suppose bile stopped neutralising the hydrochloric acid from the stomach. Use the lock-and-key model to say what would happen to enzymes in the small intestine.
kf2.note: The intestinal enzymes would stop working. Without bile, the hydrochloric acid would not be neutralised, so the small intestine would not have the alkaline conditions its enzymes need. That pH is too extreme for them. Their active sites would change shape, which is denaturation. The substrate would no longer fit the active site, like a key that no longer fits its lock. If you only said the enzymes slow down, you missed the change of shape.

dg1.tip: Sketch the digestive system from memory. Label the stomach, liver, gall bladder, pancreas, small intestine and large intestine with one job each.
dg1.note: A good sketch runs as one tube from the mouth to the anus. Check that you gave each organ its own job. The stomach churns food and adds acid. The liver makes bile. The gall bladder stores bile. The pancreas produces enzymes. The small intestine absorbs soluble products into the blood. The large intestine absorbs water. A common slip is saying the liver stores bile, or putting the gall bladder's job on the liver.

cs1.tip: Explain to a Year 7 how bile emulsifying fats helps lipase work, using an everyday comparison, in 30 words or fewer.
cs1.note: A strong answer says that bile breaks large fat droplets into smaller ones. This gives more surface area, so lipase has more places to work and breaks the fat down faster. Your everyday comparison should show that small pieces expose more surface than one big lump. If you said bile breaks down or digests the fat itself, that is the trap. Lipase does the breaking down, and bile only splits the droplets.
